item.title: Why Feeling Safe Can Be Complicated for Queer People
item.description:
Relationships

Why Feeling Safe Can Be Complicated for Queer People

The lasting impact of growing up queer in a world that wasn't always safe.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling accepted today does not automatically erase earlier experiences of stigma, shame, or exclusion.
  • Minority stress can shape how queer people experience intimacy, desire, and emotional safety.
  • Hypervigilance that once served a protective purpose can persist long after external circumstances improve.

As a psychologist and sex therapist, I often work with queer people who have done a tremendous amount of personal growth to be and express their authentic selves. In this post, I use the term “queer” as an inclusive umbrella term while recognizing that not everyone identifies with it. The folks I work with may be out to their families, accepted by their friends, living in supportive communities, and in loving relationships. On the surface, their lives may look very different from the environments in which they grew up.

Yet many still find themselves struggling with anxiety, hypervigilance, shame, self-doubt, or difficulty fully relaxing into intimacy. This can feel confusing. "If I'm accepted now, why do I still feel this way?" It is a question I hear often, particularly during Pride season. Pride is a celebration of visibility, authenticity, and belonging. But for many queer people, the deeper work involves learning how to feel safe enough to fully inhabit their lives, relationships, bodies, and desires.

How Early Life Messages Shape Feelings of Safety

Many queer people grow up receiving messages, either directly or indirectly, that some aspect of who they are is unacceptable. Sometimes those messages are explicit. Sometimes they are subtle. A child may never hear the words "being queer is wrong" and still learn that certain feelings, expressions, identities, or relationships are safer left unspoken. It could be a look on their parent’s face or the tension in their grandparent’s body when they dress a certain way.

Children are remarkably perceptive. They learn what is welcomed, what is tolerated, and what creates disconnection. They learn when it feels safe to express themselves and when it feels safer to hide. Over time, these experiences leave an imprint. Psychologists often refer to the cumulative impact of these experiences as minority stress. Minority stress refers to the additional burden that can come from living in a world where aspects of your identity have been stigmatized, questioned, marginalized, or made unsafe.

Importantly, minority stress is not limited to overt discrimination. It can also involve years of anticipating rejection, monitoring how others might respond, editing parts of yourself to fit in, or wondering whether acceptance is conditional. For many queer people, these experiences do not simply disappear once acceptance is found. The body remembers, which is why it can take a while for the body to catch up to the mind.

Someone may know intellectually that their partner loves them and still feel anxious when conflict arises. Someone else may deeply desire intimacy but find themselves pulling away when relationships become emotionally close. Others may continue struggling with shame around desire, pleasure, vulnerability, or self-expression despite consciously embracing their identity.

These reactions are not signs of weakness. Often, they are remnants of earlier adaptations that once helped a person navigate environments that felt unsafe. This is one reason emotional safety can feel surprisingly complicated.

What Does Emotional Safety Really Mean for Queer People?

Many people think safety means the absence of threat. But emotional safety is more than that. Emotional safety is the experience of being able to exist as yourself without constantly monitoring, editing, protecting, or abandoning parts of who you are. For queer people, that experience can be profoundly healing because it directly challenges years of learning that authenticity might come at a cost.

The same dynamics of safety and threat often show up in sexuality. Sexuality does not develop in a vacuum. It develops within families, communities, cultures, religious systems, and social environments. When shame, secrecy, fear, or stigma become intertwined with sexuality, those experiences can continue shaping how a person relates to desire and intimacy long after they consciously reject those messages. This is one reason self-acceptance and embodiment are not always the same thing.

A person may fully accept themselves intellectually while still discovering what it feels like to be safe in their body, safe in desire, safe in vulnerability, and safe in intimate connection. Healing often involves more than changing beliefs. It involves creating new experiences of connection. It involves being known and accepted for who you are. It involves setting boundaries and discovering that relationships can survive them. It involves expressing needs without fear of rejection. And it involves learning, over time, that authenticity does not inevitably lead to abandonment.

Being in your body is not necessarily a dramatic experience. Often, it looks surprisingly ordinary. It may be noticing that your shoulders have relaxed, that you can take a full breath, or that you are aware of your own feelings and desires rather than focusing entirely on someone else's reactions. It may be the ability to stay connected to yourself during intimacy, conflict, or vulnerability without immediately moving into self-protection, people-pleasing, or withdrawal. For many people, embodiment is less about achieving a particular feeling and more about learning to notice what is already happening inside them.

Over time, these experiences help teach something new. Connection does not require hiding. Intimacy does not require self-erasure. Safety is not simply the absence of danger. It is the presence of enough acceptance, attunement, and belonging to fully be one’s self.

Questions to Reflect on Your Relationship With Safety

If you are reflecting on your own relationship to safety, consider the following questions:

  • Are there parts of yourself you still monitor or edit in relationships?
  • When conflict arises, do you expect connection or rejection?
  • Do you feel able to express your needs, desires, and boundaries openly?
  • What helps you feel most fully yourself with another person?
  • What does safety actually feel like in your body?

For many queer people, healing is not simply about becoming more visible. It is about becoming more fully present and embodied. It is the gradual process of learning that who you are does not have to be hidden, managed, or earned in order to belong. And perhaps that is one of the deepest meanings of Pride: not only being seen by others, but finally feeling safe enough to be seen by yourself.

item.title: 4 Types of Present-but-Absent Fathers
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

4 Types of Present-but-Absent Fathers

Distant, controlling, or self-absorbed fathers can leave lasting marks.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Distant, reactive, controlling, or self-absorbed fathers may leave children emotionally unseen.
  • Healthy fathers offer consistency, safety, accountability, and emotional connection.
  • Healing does not require denial, forced gratitude, or pretending the relationship is closer than it is.
Source: AI generated

Father’s Day is one of the most widely observed holidays in the U.S., though it tends to receive less cultural attention than Mother’s Day. Like Mother’s Day, it can stir a complicated mix of emotions.

For some, Father’s Day is simple. It is a day of gratitude, celebration, and connection. For others, it is emotionally complicated because the person being celebrated was present in some ways but unavailable in others. He may have provided financially, lived in the home, or appeared responsible to the outside world, while still being emotionally distant, reactive, controlling, self-absorbed, or immature behind closed doors.

Present and healthy fathers are often less dramatic than people expect. They are not perfect. Their strengths lie in emotional availability, consistency, accountability, and safety. They show up, not only physically but emotionally. They can regulate themselves, repair when they cause harm, and make room for their child’s individuality.

The more complicated fathers are harder to name. They may not fit the obvious image of absence or abuse, but their children may still carry lasting emotional wounds. These fathers often struggle with empathy, accountability, emotional regulation, vulnerability, consistency, and attunement to their children’s needs.

This is where Father’s Day can become painful: when the father was there, but not fully available.

The Distant Father

The distant father is physically present but emotionally absent. He may be a provider. He may offer physical safety. He may attend events, live in the home, or fulfill certain responsibilities. Yet he rarely asks meaningful questions, offers comfort, expresses affection, or shows sustained emotional interest.

These fathers often believe that being in the home is enough. They may watch television, play video games, scroll on their phones, work long hours, or remain emotionally unavailable even when sitting in the same room. Conversations may stay practical, corrective, or superficial. Deeper conversations may only occur when rules have been broken, and punishment is required.

The Reactive Father

The reactive father responds to stress, frustration, or disagreement with anger, irritation, defensiveness, withdrawal, or mood swings. His emotional state can shape the entire household.

In these families, wives, partners, and children often learn to monitor their father's mood, avoid triggers, and shrink themselves to keep the peace. The home may look stable from the outside, while everyone inside is walking on eggshells.

These fathers may blame others for their outbursts. They may insist they were “just tired,” “just joking,” “not yelling,” or “pushed too far.” Instead of taking accountability, they make others responsible for managing their emotions. For children, this is called parentification.

The Controlling Father

The controlling father often confuses control with care. He may demand unwavering obedience, restrict independence, criticize choices, and treat the child as an extension of himself rather than a separate person.

These fathers are often authoritarian in their parenting style, marked by high control and low emotional responsiveness. This is the “because I said so” approach to parenting. Questions are interpreted as disrespect. Autonomy is treated as rebellion. The father’s authority becomes more important than the child’s development.

Criticism may be disguised as guidance. Harshness may be framed as discipline. Emotional distance may be labeled as a strength. The child may be punished not only for misbehavior, but for having opinions, preferences, emotions, or boundaries.

Authoritarian parenting may teach children how to obey, but it does not always teach them how to think, communicate, regulate emotions, or trust themselves.

The Self-Absorbed Father

The self-centered father prioritizes his own needs, image, comfort, and ego. He may have a carefully curated public identity as successful, respected, generous, or admirable. Inside the family, however, his children may feel unseen unless they are affirming him.

These fathers may expect admiration and become defensive or resentful when they feel criticized. Their children may learn never to say anything that could embarrass them, challenge them, or puncture the image they want others to see.

Some self-absorbed fathers compete with their children rather than celebrate them. Others use their children’s accomplishments as proof of their own success. A child’s milestone becomes another opportunity for the father to center himself.

Even during difficult moments, his pain may be prioritized. A child’s struggles may be minimized because his feelings, stress, or sacrifices are treated as more important.

Children of self-absorbed fathers may grow up feeling useful, impressive, or responsible, but not truly known.

Why Emotional Absence Leaves Lasting Marks

Present-but-emotionally-absent fathers can be especially confusing. It is often easier to understand the pain of a father who left, or the fear caused by a father who was overtly abusive. The more confusing wound comes from the father who was physically present but emotionally unavailable.

Adult children of emotionally neglectful or emotionally immature fathers may struggle with people-pleasing, emotional avoidance, fear of conflict, difficulty trusting others, overachievement, hypervigilance, or attraction to emotionally unavailable partners. What helped them survive childhood may later interfere with intimacy, self-expression, and emotional safety in adulthood.

Why Father’s Day Can Feel Like a Trigger

As an adult, holidays can activate grief over what was missing in childhood. Father’s Day cards, sermons, social media posts, commercials, and family gatherings can become reminders of a relationship that never felt as safe, close, or loving as it was supposed to be.

The grief is not always about what happened. Sometimes it is about what did not happen.

It is the conversation that never came.

The apology that was never offered.

The protection that was inconsistent.

The interest that was absent.

The affection that felt conditional.

That kind of grief can be difficult to explain, especially when others say, “At least he was there.”

But physical presence is not the same as emotional presence.

Healing Without Denial

Healing does not require denial. It does not require pretending the relationship was closer, safer, or healthier than it actually was. It does not require minimizing what happened simply because someone else had it worse.

You can acknowledge what your father provided while still telling the truth about what he could not give.

The relationship you have with your father in adulthood is a reflection of the relationship he built with you in childhood. That does not mean change is impossible, but it does mean that closeness cannot be demanded simply because of biology, tradition, or a holiday.

In adulthood, you get to redefine the relationship. You can grieve what you never had. You can set limits around your time, attention, emotional labor, and access. You can decide what kind of contact feels healthy, honest, and sustainable.

You Are Allowed to Tell the Truth

Father’s Day does not have to force emotional dishonesty. You do not have to perform gratitude that erases your grief. You do not have to pretend a relationship is simple when it has been complicated for years.

Healing may bring conflict, confusion, guilt, and pressure from others. You may wrestle with what you think you “should” do versus what feels emotionally honest.

But telling the truth about your experience is not disrespect. It is clarity.
